nameStory: Atlantic mackerel gets its name from the Old French 'maquerel,' though the exact origin is debated among linguists. Some say it comes from a word meaning 'spotted' or 'marked,' referring to those distinctive wavy black lines across its back. Here in New England, you'll often hear it called 'Boston mackerel' since Boston's fishing fleet has long prized these silvery speedsters.
description: The Atlantic mackerel is a sleek, torpedo-shaped fish built for speed in New England's coastal waters. Its steel-blue back is decorated with distinctive wavy black lines, while its belly shines bright silver. Most mackerel you'll encounter are about a foot long, though some can reach up to two feet. These fish are true ocean wanderers, appearing near our shores in spring and summer before heading to deeper waters when temperatures drop.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Steel-blue back with distinctive wavy black lines running across it like zebra stripes, contrasting sharply with a bright silvery-white belly that feels smooth and slippery to touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that tapers toward both ends, feeling firm and muscular when handled, with a distinctly pointed snout

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins on the back with a large gap between them, plus small triangular finlets behind both the back and belly fins that feel like tiny rigid flags

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically around 12 inches long for mature fish, though some reach 24 inches, with a solid, dense feel that's heavier than you'd expect for their size

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in open ocean waters near the surface, often traveling in large schools that create silvery flashes visible from boats

habitat: Atlantic mackerel cruise New England's coastal waters from the surface down to about 660 feet deep, preferring the open ocean over nearshore areas. You'll find them in the cooler waters of the Gulf of Maine, around Cape Cod, and offshore from Rhode Island and Connecticut. They favor areas where ocean currents bring together small fish and plankton, often appearing where fishing boats work the continental shelf.

seasonality.spring: Mackerel arrive in New England waters as temperatures warm, moving inshore to spawn. This is prime fishing season as large schools appear near the coast.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for mackerel fishing, with fish staying close to shore in surface waters. Their distinctive markings are most vivid during these warmer months.
seasonality.fall: As water temperatures drop, mackerel begin their migration offshore and southward. Numbers near shore start to decline by late fall.
seasonality.winter: Mackerel move to deeper, warmer waters far offshore and south of New England. Rarely encountered in coastal waters during this season.

funFact: A single female Atlantic mackerel can release up to 450,000 eggs in one spawning season - that's nearly half a million potential baby fish from just one mom!
confusionNotes: Atlantic mackerel are sometimes confused with their cousin, the Atlantic chub mackerel, but chub mackerel have spots on their bellies while true Atlantic mackerel have clean silver bellies. Remember: wavy lines on back plus clean silver belly equals Atlantic mackerel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Boston mackerel' locally, this is the same species found across the North Atlantic, from Norway to North Carolina. The strong, oily flavor that makes them prized for smoking also means they don't keep fresh as long as other fish - buy them with bright, clear eyes and no 'fishy' smell.
compareHints: Atlantic mackerel can be distinguished from Atlantic chub mackerel by their completely silver bellies - chub mackerel have dark spots scattered across their undersides. Atlantic mackerel also tend to have more pronounced wavy black lines on their backs and a slightly more streamlined body shape. Both are members of the same genus but the clean belly is the dead giveaway for Atlantic mackerel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Atlantic chub mackerel differs from its close relative, the Atlantic mackerel, by having a slightly deeper, more rounded body and more irregular wavy lines on its sides rather than straight bars.
